title: 11+ Online Tuition: A Parent’s Guide to Targeted Preparation
description: A parent guide to 11+ preparation: check the actual local or school test, diagnose gaps, build English, maths and reasoning skills, and use timed practice well.

children: There is no single national 11+ paper. The subjects, question styles, timings and test provider can vary between grammar-school areas, local authorities, consortiums and individual schools. Good preparation therefore starts with the actual admissions test your child will sit, then builds the knowledge, reasoning, accuracy and confidence that test requires.
Start with the Actual 11+ Test

Depending on the area or school, an 11+ test may include one or more of English, maths, verbal reasoning and non-verbal reasoning, and the balance of questions can differ. Before buying large sets of papers or starting a fixed programme, check the admissions authority or target school for the current test format and any official familiarisation material.
Useful preparation should be built around:
Target-test requirements:
Confirm the provider, subjects, timings, question format and official guidance for the school or area.
Baseline assessment:
Separate curriculum gaps from unfamiliar question types, weak accuracy, vocabulary issues or time pressure.
Skill development:
Teach comprehension, vocabulary, arithmetic, problem solving and reasoning in the proportions the target test requires.
Familiarisation:
Introduce unfamiliar formats deliberately so the child understands how to approach them before heavy timed practice.
Review and feedback:
Keep track of recurring error patterns and revisit them until the child can correct them independently.
The key is alignment, not volume. Twenty generic practice papers are less useful than a smaller amount of work that addresses the right test and the child’s actual weaknesses.

What Good 11+ Tuition Should Look Like

Effective 11+ tuition should respond to evidence from the student’s work. A tutor needs to know whether a wrong answer came from missing curriculum knowledge, unfamiliar reasoning, weak vocabulary, poor inference, rushed reading, calculation errors or time pressure before deciding what to teach next.
Diagnostic Teaching

Lessons should use mistakes as evidence. Rather than moving from worksheet to worksheet, the tutor should identify patterns, explain the underlying skill, model an approach and then check whether the student can apply it independently to a new question.
Appropriate Pace and Challenge

Preparation should stretch a child without turning every session into a high-pressure mock test. Difficulty and timing should increase as skills become secure, with enough untimed teaching for genuinely new material.
Vocabulary, Reading and Core Maths

Strong comprehension, vocabulary, arithmetic and problem-solving foundations matter across many selective tests. These underlying skills are more transferable than memorising shortcuts for isolated question types.
Reasoning Where the Test Requires It

Verbal and non-verbal reasoning deserve focused familiarisation when they form part of the target test, particularly because children may not meet these question types regularly at school. They should not, however, dominate preparation for an exam that places greater weight elsewhere.
Timed Practice at the Right Stage

Timed work becomes useful once the child understands the content and question types. It can then reveal problems with pacing, checking and decision-making. Constant full-paper testing too early can measure weaknesses repeatedly without actually teaching them.
How to Choose 11+ Tuition for Your Child

Ask for specific answers about how the tuition will be matched to your child and the target school or area. The strongest signs are a clear diagnostic process, relevant test knowledge and an explanation of how progress will be reviewed.
Knowledge of the target test:
The tutor should establish the actual school, consortium or local test rather than assume every 11+ is identical.
Proper diagnosis:
Early work should reveal precise strengths and weaknesses instead of simply generating a score.
Clear teaching:
The tutor should be able to model methods, explain reasoning and adapt explanations when a child is stuck.
Appropriate challenge:
Work should stretch the child progressively without replacing teaching with constant high-pressure testing.
Useful feedback:
Feedback should identify what went wrong, why it went wrong and what will be practised next.
Evidence of progress:
Over time, the child should show greater accuracy, independence, understanding and control under suitable time limits.

Specific answers are more useful than broad promises of confidence or success. No tutor can guarantee an offer, because admissions depend on the test, the school’s arrangements and the performance of the wider cohort.

How Parents Can Support 11+ Preparation

Parents do not need to recreate school at home. A small amount of consistent, purposeful practice is usually easier to sustain than long bursts of cramming, particularly when mistakes are reviewed rather than simply scored.
Use short, consistent practice:
Regular focused work is easier to sustain than occasional long sessions.
Read widely:
Fiction and non-fiction reading supports comprehension, vocabulary and inference.
Build vocabulary in context:
Discuss unfamiliar words, roots, synonyms and precise meanings rather than learning disconnected lists only.
Keep core maths fluent:
Mental arithmetic and secure written methods reduce unnecessary cognitive load in problem-solving questions.
Review mistakes:
Ask why an answer was wrong and redo similar questions later instead of recording only the score.
Avoid over-testing:
Full papers are useful at the right stage, but they should not replace teaching and targeted practice.
Share relevant school information:
Recent work or teacher feedback can help a tutor distinguish entrance-test issues from wider curriculum gaps.
Calm consistency is more useful than constant testing. The goal is to make important skills increasingly secure while keeping preparation manageable for a Year 5 or Year 6 pupil.
Skills That Matter Beyond the Test

Well-designed preparation should strengthen useful school skills even when the immediate goal is an entrance exam. Reading carefully, explaining reasoning, checking work and working independently remain valuable regardless of the eventual admissions outcome.
Reading stamina:
sustained attention to increasingly demanding texts and questions.
Vocabulary:
a broader and more precise understanding of words in context.
Problem solving:
selecting and applying methods rather than relying on one rehearsed procedure.
Accuracy and checking:
noticing avoidable errors and developing reliable checking routines.
Independent study habits:
attempting unfamiliar work, reflecting on mistakes and using feedback constructively.
That broader value is another reason to prioritise genuine teaching over endless test rehearsal. Preparation should leave a child more capable, not merely more familiar with one stack of papers.

Effective 11+ preparation begins by identifying the actual test, then diagnosing the child’s starting point, teaching the relevant skills, practising them deliberately and reviewing errors. Tuition can support that process, but it should never be presented as a guarantee of admission.
